chunks: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: There is no goodness in one who does not love to amass wealth from halal (permissible) means — with which he protects his dignity, fulfils his debt, and maintains his family ties.

key_terms.جَمْعَ الْمَالِ: Accumulation of wealth — here specifically from lawful sources, presented positively
key_terms.حَلَال: That which is permissible under Islamic law; the qualifier distinguishing licit from illicit gain
key_terms.صِلَةُ الرَّحِمِ: Maintaining kinship ties, a well-established Islamic duty connected here to economic capacity
key_terms.يَكُفُّ وَجْهَهُ: Literally 'to stop/restrain his face' — an idiom for preserving one's dignity and avoiding the humiliation of begging

ai.seo_question: Is seeking wealth and financial independence encouraged in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) affirmed the legitimacy and even virtue of seeking lawful wealth, challenging any tendency toward false asceticism or willful poverty. The teaching identifies three constructive uses of wealth: preserving one's dignity (avoiding begging or dependence), discharging financial obligations, and nurturing family bonds. The original audience, living in a society where economic hardship could lead to dishonour, would have understood this as a balanced, worldly ethic grounded in Islamic values.
